title: Traction
subtitle: Get a Grip on Your Business
author: Gino Wickman
why_it_matters: It gave small companies a full operating routine — meetings, numbers, priorities, roles — instead of another book about vision. Thousands of firms now run some version of it. Treat it as a practitioner's system rather than researched truth: there is no independent evidence base behind the framework.

crux.headline: Rhythm beats brilliance in a small company
crux.body: A small business rarely dies of bad strategy. It dies of a hundred good intentions that never got a slot in the week. So install the plumbing: one page of direction everyone can repeat, a handful of priorities per quarter, a short sheet of weekly numbers, a meeting with a fixed shape, and one list where every problem waits its turn. Dull, repeatable machinery is what turns an owner's ideas into a company that runs without them.

sparks.hook: Your company is not short of ideas. It is short of a week that repeats.
sparks.insight: Small companies rarely fail because the founder ran out of good ideas. They fail because nothing in the calendar forces the good idea to become a shipped thing. An operating system fixes that by making a few rhythms non-negotiable: a yearly direction, a ninety-day set of priorities, a weekly meeting with a fixed shape, a short list of numbers checked every Monday. None of it is clever. Its power is that it runs whether or not anyone feels inspired, which is most weeks.
sparks.why: Founders over-index on strategy because strategy is fun and cheap. Execution is repetitive and dull, so it gets skipped first — which is exactly why a system that runs without motivation outperforms one that needs it.
sparks.apply: Block the same ninety minutes every week for a leadership meeting and do not move it for a customer, a fire or a flight. Protect the slot for a full quarter.

sparks.hook: If eight people describe the plan eight ways, you do not have a plan.
sparks.insight: A strategy that lives in the founder's head is a private hobby. The test is not whether you can explain it. It is whether every leader can state, without prompting, what the company is for, who it serves, what it refuses to do, and what has to be true in three years. Getting there means writing it on a single page and repeating it far past the point where you are bored of your own words. Boredom in the leader is roughly the point where the message starts landing with everyone else.
sparks.why: Repetition is not condescension. People hear a message intermittently, in fragments, while distracted by their own work, so the sender always hits saturation long before the audience reaches comprehension.
sparks.apply: Ask each leader separately to write the company's three-year picture in five lines, then compare the answers side by side without editing them.

sparks.hook: Two different questions: is this the right person, and is this the right seat?
sparks.insight: Hiring pain usually comes from collapsing two separate judgements into one. The first is about values: does this person behave the way the company needs, regardless of role. The second is about fit: do they understand the job, actually want it, and have the capacity to do it at the size you are becoming. A great person in the wrong seat looks like a performance problem and gets managed as one, which fixes nothing. Separate the questions and the right action becomes obvious — coach, move, or part ways.
sparks.why: Values misfits damage a team even when they perform, and seat misfits fail even when they are loved. Treating both as underperformance produces the wrong intervention about half the time.
sparks.apply: List your team on paper. Mark each person twice: values fit yes or no, and seat fit yes or no. Act only on the boxes that are honestly no.

carousel.title: Name the behaviours
carousel.body: Write the three or four behaviours the company actually rewards, drawn from your best people rather than from a poster. Vague values like integrity fail this test because nobody ever fails them.

carousel.title: Score people, not roles
carousel.body: Rate each person against those behaviours with evidence, not impressions. One recent example either way is enough. Ratings without examples turn into popularity contests.

carousel.title: Test the seat separately
carousel.body: Ask three things about the job: do they grasp it, do they want it, and can they carry it at next year's volume. A no on any one is a different problem with a different fix.

carousel.title: Choose within a quarter
carousel.body: Decide to coach, move or exit, and set a date. Leaving a known mismatch unresolved teaches everyone that the standards are decorative.

sparks.hook: A year is too long to plan and a week is too short. Ninety days is the unit.
sparks.insight: Annual goals rot quietly. By March the world has moved and nobody remembers what was agreed in January, so the year ends in a scramble. Quarterly priorities are short enough that you can still see the finish line and long enough to finish something real. The discipline is the number: three to seven for the company, and a handful each for a person. Anything longer is a wish list, because a list of fifteen priorities is a way of saying nothing is a priority while sounding organised.
sparks.why: Ninety days sits inside most people's planning horizon, so commitments stay vivid. Cutting the list creates the scarcity that forces the actual trade-off conversation, which is the part organisations avoid.
sparks.apply: Choose at most five things that must be finished this quarter, name one owner per item, and write the date each one is done by.

sparks.hook: A monthly profit report tells you about a month you can no longer influence.
sparks.insight: Financial statements are a lagging record of decisions already made. What a small company needs instead is a short weekly sheet of leading numbers — calls booked, quotes sent, jobs completed, cash collected, tickets open — each with a name and a target next to it. Five to fifteen lines, looked at every week by the same people. When a number goes off, you find out inside seven days instead of at the month-end review, and the fix is still cheap.
sparks.why: Leading measures move before the outcome does, so they buy reaction time. The weekly cadence matters as much as the metrics: monthly review means the average problem runs unchecked for a fortnight.
sparks.apply: Build a single sheet of no more than fifteen weekly numbers, each owned by one person with a target, and review it at the top of every leadership meeting.

sparks.hook: Your weekly meeting is a status update. That is why everyone hates it.
sparks.insight: Most leadership meetings spend their time on information that could have been an email, then run out of clock exactly when the hard thing surfaces. Flip the ratio. Keep reporting to a few tight minutes — numbers, priorities, headline news — and give the bulk of the hour to a ranked list of real problems, working them one at a time until they are actually resolved. Same day, same time, same shape, every week. Predictability is what lets people bring the awkward item instead of saving it.
sparks.why: A fixed agenda removes the negotiation about what the meeting is for, and the fixed slot removes the negotiation about whether it happens. Both negotiations are where good meeting habits usually die.
sparks.apply: Rewrite next week's agenda so at least half the time is reserved for solving a ranked list of problems, and cut every item that is pure reporting.

carousel.title: Start with the numbers
carousel.body: Run the weekly scorecard fast. Each owner says on track or off track, nothing more. Discussion of an off number goes to the problem list, not into the reporting section.

carousel.title: Check the quarter
carousel.body: Each priority owner says on track or off. Again, no explanation. The point is to surface drift early, not to hold a defence hearing in front of colleagues.

carousel.title: Build the list
carousel.body: Collect every problem worth the group's time, including new ones raised in the room, then rank the top three by the cost of leaving them alone for another week.

carousel.title: Solve one at a time
carousel.body: Take the first item, agree what the real problem is, argue it once, then decide. Move to the next only when someone owns an action with a date.

carousel.title: Close with actions
carousel.body: Read back every commitment made and who owns it. A meeting that ends without a written list of owners and dates has produced conversation, not progress.

sparks.hook: Half your arguments are about the symptom, not the thing underneath it.
sparks.insight: Teams burn hours debating a surface complaint — this client is difficult, the handover is messy — while the actual problem sits one layer down and never gets named. Before anyone proposes a solution, force the group to agree in one sentence on what the problem is. It usually takes several attempts and it feels like a delay. It is not. Once the real issue is stated plainly, the answer is often obvious and the discussion collapses from forty minutes to five.
sparks.why: Solution talk is more comfortable than problem talk because it feels productive. The cost is that a group can agree enthusiastically on a fix for something that was never the cause.
sparks.apply: Next time an argument passes ten minutes, stop and make someone state the problem in one sentence everyone accepts before any solution is allowed.

sparks.hook: Write down the annoying thing instead of discussing it right now.
sparks.insight: Most small companies have no place to put a problem, so problems get raised whenever they are felt — mid-corridor, mid-project, mid-someone-else's meeting. Keeping a single visible list changes the economics. Anything that is not on fire goes on the list and waits for the weekly slot where it can be properly argued and closed. Interruptions drop, the same complaint stops recirculating, and the list itself becomes an honest picture of what the company is avoiding.
sparks.why: A capture point separates noticing from solving. Without one, urgency sets the agenda, and urgency is a poor judge of importance in a business that is not actually on fire.
sparks.apply: Open one shared list today, name it plainly, and require that anything raised outside a genuine fire goes there first and gets worked in the weekly meeting.

sparks.hook: Design the seats your company needs, then see who fits them.
sparks.insight: The usual org chart is a map of who you happened to hire. Reverse it. Sketch the functions the business genuinely needs at the size you are heading toward, write the three to five outcomes each one owns, and only then put names in boxes. Founders find this uncomfortable because their own name lands in four boxes at once, which is precisely the diagnosis. Every function with no clear owner is a place where work quietly becomes nobody's job and shows up later as a fire.
sparks.why: Structure should follow the work, not the people, or you end up designing the company around the strengths and blind spots of whoever joined first. That constraint gets more expensive every year.
sparks.apply: Draw the structure your business needs eighteen months from now with outcomes written under each box, leave the names off, and fill them in last.

sparks.hook: You do not need a process manual. You need seven processes written thinly.
sparks.insight: Documentation projects die because people try to capture everything. The useful version is smaller: identify the handful of processes the business actually runs on — how you win work, deliver it, bill it, hire — and write only the steps that must not vary. A page each, not a binder. Then make everyone follow the same version. Consistency is what lets you hand work to a newer and less experienced person without quality collapsing, which is the only way an owner ever gets their week back.
sparks.why: Variation is where quality and margin leak. Capturing the critical few steps removes most of the variation at a fraction of the cost of full documentation, which almost nobody ever finishes anyway.
sparks.apply: Name your core processes on one page this week, then have each owner draft only the steps that must never change. Cap each at a single page.

actions: Write your company's direction on a single page, then ask every leader to reproduce it from memory a week later and fix whatever nobody could recall.
Cut next quarter's plan to five finished outcomes with one named owner and one due date each, and delete everything else from the list.
Build a fifteen-line weekly scorecard with a target and an owner per line, and start every leadership meeting by reading it in under five minutes.
Run the same meeting agenda for eight consecutive weeks before judging it, and keep a written list of every problem the company keeps postponing.
not_for_you_if: You run a large or highly technical organisation, or you find prescriptive branded frameworks with trademarked tool names harder to take seriously than plain advice.

verification.notes: Self-published in 2007 and widely reissued by BenBella in 2011; the framework is the Entrepreneurial Operating System. It is a practitioner framework with no independent research base. All prose here is original.

title: The E-Myth Revisited
subtitle: Why Most Small Businesses Don't Work and What to Do About It
author: Michael E. Gerber
why_it_matters: It named the trap that swallows most small businesses: the skilled person who starts a company and ends up with a demanding job instead of an asset. Its cure — build the business as a repeatable model, not a personal performance — became standard advice for every service firm since.

crux.headline: You are building a job, not a business
crux.body: Being good at the work is the worst possible reason to start a company doing it, because the skill that earns the first customers is the skill that traps you. A business is an asset only if it can produce the same result without you in the room. So stop being the best worker and start designing the thing a competent stranger could run: steps written down, a defined standard, results you can measure. Your job is to design the machine, not to be its best moving part.

sparks.hook: Being brilliant at the work is a common reason a business fails.
sparks.insight: The baker opens a bakery, the coder starts an agency, the plumber goes independent. Each one is excellent at the craft and assumes that is the hard part. It is not. Running a company is a different job — selling, hiring, pricing, chasing money, deciding — and craft skill offers no help with any of it. Worse, the founder keeps retreating into the work they love because it is the only part that feels competent, while the actual business quietly goes unmanaged.
sparks.why: Technical skill and enterprise skill are unrelated capabilities. Competence in one produces the confidence to attempt the other, which is why the assumption survives so long before the business finally tests it.
sparks.apply: List every hour of last week as craft work or company work. If company work is under a fifth of your time, block one morning a week for it now.

sparks.hook: Three people live inside every founder, and two of them are usually starving.
sparks.insight: There is the part of you that wants to build something new, the part that wants order and process, and the part that just wants to do the work today. Most founders are heavily weighted to the last one, so the visionary gets a few excited hours a year and the organiser never gets any. The result is a company that lurches between new ideas and daily firefighting with no structure in between. The fix is not personality change; it is booking time for the roles you neglect.
sparks.why: The typology is a useful heuristic drawn from decades of consulting, not a validated psychological model. Treat it as a way to notice which mode you default to, rather than as a personality test.
sparks.apply: Book two hours this week for the organising role — writing down one process — and treat it as unmovable as a meeting with your largest client.

carousel.title: Spot your default
carousel.body: Over one week, tag each block of work as inventing, organising or doing. The tag that dominates is your default mode, and the two thin ones are where your company is weakest.

carousel.title: Feed the organiser
carousel.body: Give the neglected organising role a fixed slot. It produces the checklists, standards and numbers that let other people do work at your quality without you present.

carousel.title: Ration the doer
carousel.body: Doing the work is not wrong, it is just unlimited. Cap it deliberately so it stops eating the hours meant for building the company itself.

carousel.title: Schedule the visionary
carousel.body: Once a quarter, spend half a day only on where this is going. Ideas do not need more of your enthusiasm; they need a slot in the calendar.

sparks.hook: Ask what the business must look like when you are not in it.
sparks.insight: Most planning starts from today and drifts forward. Try the opposite. Describe the company as it must work when you are no longer required — how a customer is served, what the standard is, who does what, how you would know it went well. That description is a specification, and everything you build from now on is either moving toward it or away from it. Founders resist this because the honest version reveals that the current business is mostly held together by their own attention.
sparks.why: A target state converts vague ambition into a design brief. Without one, every operational decision defaults to whatever keeps this week running, which reliably deepens the founder's dependence.
sparks.apply: Write one page describing how the business runs during a week you are completely unreachable. Then list the three things that would break first.

sparks.hook: Build it as though you will open nine more copies of it.
sparks.insight: The useful test is to imagine the business as one of many identical units, each run by an ordinary manager, none of them you. It forces you to write down what is currently improvised: the exact way a job is quoted, the way a call is answered, the standard for finished work. You will probably never open a second site. That is fine — the point of the exercise is that it exposes every part of the operation that only functions because you personally are watching it.
sparks.why: The franchise thought experiment is a design constraint, not a business plan. Its value is diagnostic: anything that cannot be handed to a competent stranger is a dependency you have not noticed yet.
sparks.apply: Pick one recurring task you do best and write it as instructions for a new hire. Then have someone else do it from your instructions without asking questions.

sparks.hook: Great results should come from the system, not from finding great people.
sparks.insight: Companies that depend on exceptional staff are fragile, because exceptional staff are rare, expensive and eventually leave. Companies that depend on well-designed routines can hire ordinary, decent people and still deliver the same result every time. That is not an insult to the staff — a good routine is how you make someone's first month look like their third year. The work is up front and unglamorous: define the standard, write the steps, train against them, then measure whether reality matches.
sparks.why: Recruiting your way out of an unreliable process only works while the labour market is kind. Designing the process transfers quality from a person, who can quit, into an asset the company owns.
sparks.apply: Take your most variable customer-facing task, define what good looks like in three measurable terms, and train one person against exactly that this week.

sparks.hook: If it is not written down, everyone runs a slightly different company.
sparks.insight: Unwritten process is not the absence of process. It is many private processes, each one drifting, none of them comparable. The moment a step exists on paper it can be taught, questioned, improved and measured against results. This is also the only honest route to delegation: handing over a task with no defined standard is not delegation, it is a lottery you will later blame the other person for losing.
sparks.why: Written steps make variation visible, and visible variation is the only kind you can fix. They also relocate the blame for failure from the person to the design, which is usually where it belongs.
sparks.apply: Write one process this week as a numbered checklist short enough to fit on one page, then follow it yourself once and correct what turns out to be wrong.

carousel.title: Pick a painful repeat
carousel.body: Choose a task that happens weekly and goes wrong often. Documenting something rare or already reliable wastes the first attempt, which is the one most likely to be finished.

carousel.title: Watch it once
carousel.body: Write the steps while doing the task, not from memory. Memory smooths over the awkward decisions, which are exactly the parts a newcomer will get wrong.

carousel.title: Cut to the must-nots
carousel.body: Keep only the steps where variation causes real damage. A checklist someone actually uses beats a manual that is complete and permanently unread.

carousel.title: Have someone else run it
carousel.body: Give the page to a person who has never done the task and let them work without help. Every question they ask marks a missing line.

sparks.hook: The customer buys how it felt, not what you technically delivered.
sparks.insight: Two firms can produce identical technical work and be experienced entirely differently, because the customer judges what they can perceive: whether the call was answered, whether the van was clean, whether anyone told them what would happen next. These details feel trivial to the person doing the skilled part, which is why they are almost never designed. Deciding them deliberately — the greeting, the follow-up, the finish — is cheap and separates you from competitors who left them to chance.
sparks.why: Buyers usually cannot evaluate technical quality, so they infer it from what they can evaluate. That inference is not irrational; it is what people do when they lack expertise, and it prices your work.
sparks.apply: Map every touch a customer has with you from first contact to final invoice, then pick the three cheapest ones to make deliberately better.

sparks.hook: Set the numbers you would need before you would ever trust a manager.
sparks.insight: You cannot hand over anything you cannot check. So decide, for each part of the business, the few numbers that tell you whether it is healthy — jobs completed on time, repeat rate, average value, days to get paid. Once those exist, delegation stops being an act of faith. You are not asking someone to be as good as you; you are asking them to hold a stated standard that both of you can see, which is far easier to hire for and to correct.
sparks.why: Measurement converts trust into evidence. Founders who refuse to delegate often have no metric, so the only available check is their own presence, which guarantees they can never leave.
sparks.apply: Choose one function and define three numbers that would let you sleep while someone else ran it. Start reporting them weekly before you hand it over.

sparks.hook: Most owners do not want a company. They want the work with better hours.
sparks.insight: There is nothing shameful about wanting a good job you control — but it is a different thing from building a business, and the two need different decisions. A job you own is optimised for your own daily satisfaction and stops being worth anything the day you stop. A business is optimised to run without you and has a sale value. Choosing one honestly is far better than drifting into the first while telling yourself you are building the second.
sparks.why: Most small-business frustration comes from wanting the freedom of an asset while making the daily choices of a self-employed craftsperson. The two strategies genuinely conflict, and picking one removes the conflict.
sparks.apply: Write down which one you actually want. If it is the business, name the first task you will stop doing yourself within the next thirty days.

sparks.hook: Your company is designed by default until you sit down and design it.
sparks.insight: Nobody decides that quoting will be chaotic or that new staff will learn by watching. Those are simply what happens when no one specifies the alternative. Every business already has a design; the only question is whether anyone chose it. Setting aside recurring time to work on the structure — even a couple of hours a week — is what moves you from a company shaped by accident to one shaped on purpose. The hours never appear on their own, because the work is never urgent.
sparks.why: Structural work has no deadline and no complaining customer attached, so it loses every scheduling contest against operational work. A protected slot is the only reliable counterweight.
sparks.apply: Put a recurring two-hour block in your diary titled with the specific structural task, not a vague label, and defend it for four consecutive weeks.

actions: Spend two hours writing how the business must work during a week you are completely unreachable, then list what would break first and fix that one thing.
Document your most variable recurring task as a one-page checklist and have someone else complete it from your page without asking you any questions.
Define three numbers for one function that would let you hand it over, and report them weekly for a month before you actually delegate anything.
Decide in writing whether you are building an asset that could be sold or a job you enjoy owning, and make your next three decisions consistent with that.
not_for_you_if: You run a business built on novel, non-repeatable work, or you want evidence and research rather than an extended consulting parable stretched across three hundred pages.

verification.notes: First published 1995 as an expanded rework of The E-Myth (1986). The three-roles typology and the franchise-prototype model are practitioner heuristics, not validated research. All prose here is original.

title: Purple Cow
subtitle: Transform Your Business by Being Remarkable
author: Seth Godin
why_it_matters: It moved marketing budget out of advertising and into the product itself, arguing that the only reliable amplifier is a thing worth talking about. Two decades of growth advice, from startup positioning to creator strategy, rests on that shift.

crux.headline: Remarkable is a product decision, not an ad budget
crux.body: Advertising works best when attention is scarce and channels are few. Neither is true any more, so shouting louder mostly raises your costs. The alternative is to build something that gives a specific group of people a reason to mention it unprompted — strange, extreme, inconvenient for someone, unmistakably not average. Safe products are invisible products. The risk you feel when you propose something odd is the same risk that makes it worth doing.

sparks.hook: Very good and completely ignored are the same commercial outcome.
sparks.insight: There is a whole category of competent products nobody mentions: the fine hotel, the reasonable insurance, the decent coffee. They are not bad. They are simply unremarkable, which means no one has any reason to tell a friend about them, so every customer has to be bought with advertising. Being slightly better than average is the most expensive position on the board, because you carry the cost of being good and none of the free distribution that comes with being talked about.
sparks.why: Word of mouth is not a reward for quality, it is a reward for tellability. Meeting the standard gives a person nothing to say, and people mostly pass on things that make them look interesting.
sparks.apply: Ask three recent customers to describe you to a friend in one sentence. If every sentence is a category description, you have a product problem.

sparks.hook: The safest-looking option in a crowded market is usually the riskiest.
sparks.insight: Committees smooth products. Each round of feedback shaves off the odd edge until what remains offends nobody and interests nobody. That process feels like risk reduction, but it trades a small chance of failure for a near-certain one: an average product in a crowded market is invisible, and invisible is fatal. The rational move in an attention-poor world is to be criticised by some people, because the same edge that repels them is what makes anyone bother mentioning you at all.
sparks.why: Consensus optimises for the least objectionable version, which is a reliable route to being ignored. The failure is slow and unattributable, so nobody in the room ever gets blamed for it.
sparks.apply: Take one product decision you softened after feedback and restore the sharp version for a limited launch to a small segment. Measure mentions, not approval.

sparks.hook: Aim at the handful of people who will actually care, not the middle.
sparks.insight: Most markets contain a small group who care intensely about the category, a large mass who are indifferent, and a tail of laggards. Advertising traditionally aimed at the mass, which is precisely the group least willing to try anything new. The alternative is to design for the obsessives — the people already looking for what you make — and let them carry the message inward to everyone else. You reach the majority through the enthusiasts, not around them.
sparks.why: Enthusiasts have both the motivation to try unproven things and the social credibility to recommend them. Marketing to indifferent people fails not because the message is weak but because the audience is not listening.
sparks.apply: Write down the most obsessive twenty customers you could possibly serve, then change one feature specifically for them even if it annoys everyone else.

carousel.title: Find the obsessives
carousel.body: Identify the people who already care most about your category. They read about it, argue about it and try new entrants first. Everyone else is downstream of them.

carousel.title: Build for them alone
carousel.body: Make the decision that serves this group best even when it makes the product worse for the indifferent majority. Half-measures end up satisfying neither group.

carousel.title: Make sharing easy
carousel.body: Give them something concrete to pass on — an artefact, a number, an unusual policy — rather than asking them to summarise your positioning on your behalf.

carousel.title: Let it spread inward
carousel.body: Resist broadening the message while the enthusiasts are still adopting. The mass follows the people it trusts, on a delay that advertising cannot shorten.

sparks.hook: Design the product so the story tells itself.
sparks.insight: If your marketing plan requires people to remember and repeat a claim, it will fail. What travels is a feature so unusual that describing the product means describing the strange thing — the ridiculous size, the impossible guarantee, the missing option everyone else has. Build the remarkable part into what you sell rather than into what you say about it, and the story becomes free and self-carrying. Advertising then has one job left: showing the right people that it exists.
sparks.why: Claims decay through retelling; structural oddities survive because they are the point of the anecdote. Note the survivorship problem though: the examples are products that worked, and plenty of strange ones fail unnoticed.
sparks.apply: Choose one dimension where you could be visibly extreme rather than competitive — speed, guarantee, narrowness, price — and push it far enough to be worth mentioning.

carousel.title: Find the boring axis
carousel.body: List the dimensions everyone in your category competes on, then note where all of you cluster. The cluster is the middle, and the middle is invisible.

carousel.title: Pick one to break
carousel.body: Choose a single dimension to take somewhere absurd rather than slightly better. Two extremes at once usually reads as chaos rather than as character.

carousel.title: Name who it annoys
carousel.body: If the change costs nobody anything, it is not extreme enough. Write down which customers you are deliberately giving up and check you can afford it.

carousel.title: Ship it small
carousel.body: Test the sharp version with a narrow audience before rebuilding the company around it. You are looking for evidence that people repeat it unprompted.

sparks.hook: Mass advertising worked because attention had nowhere else to go.
sparks.insight: For a few decades a company could buy its way to fame: a handful of channels, a captive audience, and money that converted reliably into awareness and then into sales. That machine is gone. Attention is fragmented, avoidable and mostly under the viewer's control, so the old ratio between spend and result no longer holds. Businesses that grew up in that era often keep spending as though it does, which is why their marketing budgets rise while their share of conversation falls.
sparks.why: The historical account is accurate: the postwar advertising economy depended on scarce channels and unavoidable ads. What replaced it rewards products people choose to look at, not ones they are merely exposed to.
sparks.apply: Compare what you spend buying attention with what you spend making the product worth mentioning. If the ratio is lopsided, move one budget line.

sparks.hook: Every remarkable thing eventually stops being remarkable.
sparks.insight: The strange feature that made you famous becomes the category standard within a few years, because competitors copy anything that visibly works. So a remarkable product is not a position you hold, it is a thing you have to keep doing. Companies that treat one breakthrough as a permanent identity slowly become the average they once stood out against, usually while still congratulating themselves on the original idea. Plan the next odd thing while the current one is still being praised.
sparks.why: Imitation compresses any advantage that is visible and cheap to copy. That is why differentiation behaves like a pipeline rather than an achievement, and why the cycle keeps getting shorter.
sparks.apply: Name the thing that made you interesting and the year it happened. If it is more than three years old, start work on the next one this quarter.

sparks.hook: Ask what you would have to change for someone to bother telling a friend.
sparks.insight: The practical test is small and brutal. Imagine a satisfied customer at dinner. What could they say about you that would be interesting to the people at the table? If the honest answer is nothing — the work was fine, the price was fair — then no amount of loyalty programmes or referral incentives will produce word of mouth, because there is nothing to carry. The design brief is not satisfaction. It is giving someone material worth using in conversation.
sparks.why: People share things that say something about themselves. Satisfaction is private and unremarkable, while a story that makes the teller look informed or amusing is socially useful and therefore travels.
sparks.apply: Write the single sentence you want a customer to say about you at dinner. If nothing in the current product makes that sentence true, change the product.

sparks.hook: Copying the leader puts you in the one place the market does not need filled.
sparks.insight: The instinct in a new market is to study whoever is winning and build something similar but cheaper. It is comforting and it almost never works, because the position is already occupied by someone with more customers, more history and lower unit costs. What markets actually reward is the gap nobody has filled: the version for a group the leader ignores, or the option that is worse on the standard axis and dramatically better on a different one.
sparks.why: Head-on imitation competes against an incumbent's accumulated advantage on their own terms. Choosing a different axis avoids that fight and gives buyers a reason to switch other than price.
sparks.apply: List what the market leader is structurally unable to offer without damaging their existing business, then build exactly one of those things.

sparks.hook: Cheap is not a difference. It is a promise you may not be able to keep.
sparks.insight: Price is the easiest lever and the least defensible one. Anyone can match it, and the moment they do you are left with a smaller margin and no other reason to be chosen. Worse, a low price sets an expectation that constrains every future decision — you can no longer afford the service, the materials or the strange feature that would have made you interesting. Competing on price is a strategy only if your cost structure is genuinely different from everybody else's.
sparks.why: Discounts are instantly copyable and permanently anchoring. Structural cost advantage is rare and usually comes from scale or a different operating model, not from simply deciding to charge less.
sparks.apply: Before your next discount, write what you would have to give up to fund it permanently. If the answer is the interesting part of the product, do not.

sparks.hook: Marketing is not the department you hand a finished product to.
sparks.insight: If marketing begins after the product is built, its only job is to describe something that was designed without any thought about whether it could be described well. That is a losing brief. The decisions that determine whether anything gets talked about — what it does, who it is for, what it deliberately does not do — are made by the people building it. Which means marketing belongs at the design table, or the marketing plan is really just an advertising budget.
sparks.why: Communication cannot add distinctiveness that the product lacks, it can only reveal it. Pushing the marketing question upstream is the only point in the process where it is still cheap to answer.
sparks.apply: Invite whoever owns marketing into your next product decision meeting and give them a veto on anything that would be impossible to describe interestingly.

actions: Ask five recent customers to describe you to a friend in one sentence, write the answers down word for word, and treat generic answers as a product fault.
Pick one dimension of your product and push it to an extreme that will visibly annoy a segment you are willing to lose, then test it with a narrow audience.
Compare this year's spend on buying attention with your spend on making the product worth mentioning, and move one budget line from the first to the second.
Name the last genuinely unusual thing you shipped and its date. If it is more than three years old, schedule the next one into this quarter's plan.
not_for_you_if: You want frameworks, data and detailed method rather than a short provocation, or you operate in a regulated market where deliberate strangeness is not available.

verification.notes: Published 2003 by Portfolio. Its argument rests on selected memorable examples rather than systematic evidence, so survivorship bias is a fair criticism of it. All prose here is original.

title: This Is Marketing
subtitle: You Can't Be Seen Until You Learn to See
author: Seth Godin
why_it_matters: It reframed marketing as the work of understanding a specific group well enough to make something they want, rather than the work of persuading strangers. That framing now shapes how most modern founders and independent creators think about finding an audience.

crux.headline: Marketing is serving a specific someone, not persuading everyone
crux.body: Start with the smallest group you could possibly serve and understand what they already want, believe and fear. Build something that moves them toward it, then earn the right to be heard by showing up consistently over a long period. Growth comes from those people telling others, which only happens if the thing genuinely changed something for them. Attention is not the goal, and it is not for sale in any way that lasts.

sparks.hook: Marketing is not what you say. It is who you decide to serve.
sparks.insight: Most marketing effort goes into wording — the headline, the campaign, the channel. That is the last five percent. The decisions that actually determine whether anything works happen earlier: who exactly this is for, what they are already trying to achieve, and what they will have to give up to switch to you. Get those right and the wording becomes almost obvious. Get them wrong and no amount of clever copy rescues it, because you are talking fluently to people who do not want the thing.
sparks.why: Copy can only amplify a fit that already exists. When the audience and the promise are mismatched, better wording simply increases the number of people who correctly conclude that this is not for them.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph describing the person you serve without using demographics, focusing entirely on what they want and what they currently do instead.

sparks.hook: Pick the smallest audience you could possibly succeed with.
sparks.insight: The instinct is to widen: more segments, more use cases, a bigger addressable market. Widening makes the promise vaguer, and a vague promise is easy to ignore. Starting narrow does the opposite — it lets you make a specific claim, build exactly the right thing, and be genuinely the best option for a group small enough to actually reach. Growth from there is a choice you make later, from a position where some people already care, rather than a hope you start with.
sparks.why: This is contested. Byron Sharp's work at the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute argues most brand growth comes from broad reach and light buyers, not deep niche loyalty. Read the narrow start as advice for the early, resource-poor stage.
sparks.apply: Define the smallest group for whom your product would be the obvious first choice, then remove one feature that exists only to appeal to somebody else.

carousel.title: Describe one person
carousel.body: Write a single real customer, not a segment: their situation, what they have already tried, what they say when it goes wrong. Segments are averages, and nobody is an average.

carousel.title: Cut until it hurts
carousel.body: Remove every group you are including out of hope rather than evidence. What remains should be small enough that you could plausibly reach most of them.

carousel.title: Make an obvious promise
carousel.body: State what changes for that group in one sentence with no hedging. If the sentence would suit a competitor equally well, it is still far too broad.

carousel.title: Earn the right to widen
carousel.body: Only expand once the first group buys, returns and refers. Broadening before that hides the fact that nobody was actually convinced yet.

sparks.hook: People do not buy what you make. They buy who it lets them become.
sparks.insight: Nobody wants the drill, the software licence or the course. They want the state on the other side: the shelf up, the team calm, the feeling of being someone who has that handled. Underneath most purchases sits a small identity claim — the kind of person who buys this. If you can name the change your customer is trying to make in their own life, and how it will look to the people around them, you can build and describe the product far more precisely than any feature list allows.
sparks.why: This restates a long-standing idea in marketing: customers hire a product for the change it produces. It holds up because features get compared while outcomes get chosen, and only one of those is a decision.
sparks.apply: Write the sentence a customer would say about themselves after using your product for six months. Then check that the product actually delivers it.

sparks.hook: Trust is built by showing up repeatedly, not by being clever once.
sparks.insight: A single brilliant campaign buys attention that evaporates. What compounds is consistency: publishing on a schedule, keeping small promises, sounding like the same organisation every time. This is slow and it looks unimpressive for months, which is why most people abandon it for another launch. But the people you want are wary, they have been marketed at all their lives, and the only signal that reliably separates you from the noise is the passage of time with no unpleasant surprises.
sparks.why: Repeated, predictable contact lowers perceived risk, and perceived risk is what stops most qualified buyers. The effect is cumulative and cannot be bought quickly, which is exactly why it is defensible.
sparks.apply: Commit to one publishing rhythm you could sustain in your worst week, not your best, and hold it for twelve weeks before judging whether it works.

carousel.title: Pick a sustainable pace
carousel.body: Choose the frequency you could hold during a bad month. A weekly rhythm kept for a year beats a daily one abandoned in March, because the promise is the product.

carousel.title: Say the same things
carousel.body: Consistency of position matters more than variety of topic. People need several exposures before they can describe what you stand for to somebody else.

carousel.title: Keep small promises
carousel.body: Deliver on time, answer messages, do what the page said you would. Small kept promises are the cheapest available evidence that the large ones are safe.

carousel.title: Wait longer than feels sane
carousel.body: Judge the work in quarters, not weeks. Reputation accumulates below the surface, and switching approach every month resets the clock every month.

sparks.hook: Status is doing quiet work behind most purchases you make.
sparks.insight: Every group has an internal pecking order and a set of signals about who is rising and who is not. Buying decisions ride on that more often than people admit — the tools, the brands, the choices that mark you as serious, or thrifty, or ahead. This is not vanity; it is how humans navigate groups. If you can see what counts as status among the people you serve, and whether they want to climb or simply to belong, you can build something that fits rather than something that quietly embarrasses them.
sparks.why: Status-seeking is well documented across social psychology and consumer research. It is uncomfortable to write into a marketing plan, which is why competitors usually leave the insight sitting on the table.
sparks.apply: Ask five customers who they compare themselves to at work. Note what they admire in those people, then check whether your product helps them look like that.

sparks.hook: Empathy means accepting that other people want things you find ridiculous.
sparks.insight: The most common marketing error is assuming customers are versions of you with less information. They are not. They have different beliefs, different constraints, different ideas about what is worth money. Real empathy is not sympathy or kindness — it is the discipline of accepting that a person can be entirely rational and still want something you would never buy. Once you stop trying to correct them, you can start building for the world as they actually see it.
sparks.why: Projection is the default setting: people estimate others' preferences by consulting their own. It is a persistent, well-documented bias, and it is fatal in a job whose whole task is predicting what someone else wants.
sparks.apply: Find one thing your customers do that irritates you, and write out the version of the story in which their behaviour is completely sensible.

sparks.hook: You cannot make someone want something. You can find people who already do.
sparks.insight: Persuasion at scale barely works. What works is search: locating the people whose existing desires point at what you are building, then making it obvious to them. That reframes the whole job. You stop trying to change minds and start trying to be found by the right ones, which means clearer positioning, sharper language and a willingness to say plainly who this is not for. Saying who it is not for is what makes the yes credible.
sparks.why: Changing a settled preference is slow and expensive; matching an existing one is fast and cheap. Most marketing budgets are spent attempting the first while calling it awareness building.
sparks.apply: Add one line to your homepage stating clearly who this is not for, and watch what it does to the quality of the enquiries you receive.

sparks.hook: Tension moves people. Manufactured anxiety just makes them close the tab.
sparks.insight: Useful marketing creates a small gap between where someone is and where they could be, and holds it open until they act. That is tension, and it is honest — the person genuinely wants the thing on the other side. Manufactured fear is different: fake scarcity, countdown timers, invented threats. It converts in the short run and costs you the only asset that compounds, which is the belief that you tell the truth. The test is whether the gap would still exist if you had never mentioned it.
sparks.why: Pressure tactics work at the margin and damage repeat purchase and referral, which is where most durable value sits. The line between tension and manipulation is whether the problem is real without you.
sparks.apply: Audit your funnel for anything urgent that is not actually true — timers, false scarcity, invented deadlines — and delete one of them this week.

sparks.hook: Your best customers were sold to by other customers, not by you.
sparks.insight: Growth that lasts is almost always transmitted person to person, which means the marketing task is to make that transmission easy. That is partly product and partly language: giving people a clear, short way to describe what you do, an obvious moment when recommending you makes sense, and a result impressive enough to be worth attaching their own name to. Nobody recommends something that might embarrass them, so reliability is itself a marketing feature.
sparks.why: A recommendation carries the recommender's credibility, so its cost to them is reputational. Products that occasionally fail generate far less word of mouth than their average quality would suggest.
sparks.apply: Write the twelve-word description you want customers to use about you, then check whether your three most recent referrals said anything close to it.

sparks.hook: If nobody would miss you, you have not really made anything yet.
sparks.insight: The clean test of whether the work matters is subtraction. If your product disappeared tomorrow, who would notice within a week, and what specifically would be worse for them? A vague answer means you have built something substitutable, and substitutable things compete on price forever. A sharp answer tells you exactly who to serve, what to protect and where to invest, because you now know the precise reason you exist to somebody.
sparks.why: Missability is a proxy for switching cost and emotional attachment at the same time. It is harder to fool yourself about than satisfaction scores, which are famously generous and weakly linked to behaviour.
sparks.apply: Ask ten customers what they would use instead if you closed tomorrow. If most name a competitor without hesitating, you have a differentiation problem.

actions: Write a one-page description of the smallest group you could serve completely, covering what they already believe and what they do instead of buying from you.
Add a plain statement of who your product is not for to your website, and track whether enquiry quality improves over the following month.
Choose a publishing rhythm you could sustain through your worst month and hold it for twelve weeks before changing anything about the approach.
Ask ten customers what they would switch to if you closed tomorrow, and use the answers to find the one thing worth being irreplaceable at.
not_for_you_if: You want measurable tactics, channel mechanics or media buying rather than a philosophy of audience and trust, or you need evidence more than aphorism.

verification.notes: Published 2018 by Portfolio. Its niche-first advice sits in genuine tension with mass-reach research from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute; both views are noted in the sparks. All prose here is original.

title: Positioning
subtitle: The Battle for Your Mind
author: Al Ries and Jack Trout
why_it_matters: It relocated marketing from the product to the customer's head, arguing that what matters is the slot you occupy in a crowded mind. The vocabulary it created — owning a position, category leadership, the mental ladder — is still how marketers talk.

crux.headline: You compete inside the customer's head, not in the market
crux.body: People cannot hold much. They keep a short mental list per category, roughly ranked, and mostly ignore everything below the top few. So the job is not to describe how good you are. It is to find a slot you can plausibly own and attach yourself to it with brutal repetition. If the good slots are taken, do not fight for them. Redefine the category until there is a slot where you are first.

sparks.hook: You are not fighting competitors. You are fighting how little anyone remembers.
sparks.insight: The average person is exposed to more brands in a day than they could name in a year, so the mind runs aggressive triage: a handful of names per category, roughly ranked, everything else discarded. Marketing that ignores this limit fails in a specific way — the message is received, understood and immediately dropped because there is nowhere to file it. Winning means offering a simple, distinctive slot the mind is willing to keep, not a complete account of your merits.
sparks.why: Memory for brands is limited and organised by category, a finding that has held up well across decades of consumer research. Complexity is the enemy because complex claims cost more to store.
sparks.apply: Write down the word or short phrase you want to own in your customer's mind. If it takes more than four words, you have not chosen yet.

sparks.hook: Being first in the mind beats being better in the product.
sparks.insight: The first credible entrant into a category tends to become the reference point everyone else is compared against, and later arrivals must dislodge a memory rather than merely win an argument. That is far harder than it sounds, because people do not enjoy revising things they already believe. This is why a technically superior product frequently loses to an earlier, worse one — the comparison is not happening on a level surface, it is happening on a surface the incumbent shaped.
sparks.why: The order-of-entry advantage is real but overstated here. Later research shows pioneers often lose to fast followers, and several famous first movers were themselves preceded by forgotten entrants.
sparks.apply: List the categories you could credibly claim to be first in by narrowing the definition, then test the narrowest one on real customers.

sparks.hook: If you cannot be first in a category, invent a category you can be first in.
sparks.insight: When every good slot is occupied, the productive move is not a better claim but a different frame. Split the category by use, by buyer, by moment, or by what you deliberately exclude, until you reach a definition where you are the obvious leader. This is not a trick if the new category is genuinely useful to buyers — narrowing usually makes your promise more specific and more believable. It becomes a trick only when the category exists solely inside your own marketing deck.
sparks.why: Reframing works because comparison sets are constructed rather than fixed. It fails when the new category has no meaning to buyers, which is how the technique degrades into an award nobody has heard of.
sparks.apply: Write five narrower definitions of your market, each excluding something real, and pick the one where you could honestly claim to be the best available choice.

carousel.title: Map the ladder
carousel.body: List who customers name first, second and third in your category today. If you are not on that list, competing on the same terms is spending money to stay invisible.

carousel.title: Find the split
carousel.body: Look for a dividing line buyers already feel: a type of user, a situation, a constraint, a value. The line has to exist in their heads before you name it.

carousel.title: Give up something
carousel.body: A category you can lead is one you narrowed by excluding real business. If the new definition costs you nothing, it is not a position, it is a slogan.

carousel.title: Repeat until dull
carousel.body: Say the same thing in the same words far past your own boredom. A position exists only when customers can repeat it back to each other without your help.

sparks.hook: The company that tries to be everything to everyone ends up owning nothing.
sparks.insight: Line extension is seductive because the numbers look free: the brand is already known, so put its name on the new thing and save on marketing. The cost is invisible and delayed. Every additional meaning attached to a name blurs the one meaning it had, and a name that stands for several things stands sharply for none. The short-term revenue arrives first and the erosion arrives years later, which is why the mistake is repeated so reliably.
sparks.why: Modern evidence complicates this. Extensions frequently succeed, especially into adjacent uses, and the blanket opposition here looks too absolute. The warning holds best where the parent brand's meaning is narrow and precise.
sparks.apply: List everything sold under your main brand name and write the single meaning each item adds. Retire or rename the one that contradicts the others.

sparks.hook: Naming yourself against the leader beats pretending they do not exist.
sparks.insight: If a category has a dominant name, ignoring it does not remove it from anyone's mind — it just leaves you undefined. Attaching yourself to the leader as the deliberate alternative borrows their recognition and hands the buyer a ready-made comparison. It works when the difference is real and you are honest about being second, and it fails when you claim the leader's position instead of a different one. You are asking for a slot next to them, not their slot.
sparks.why: Contrast makes an unfamiliar option easier to place, because the mind stores it against something it already holds. The risk is amplifying the leader's name while your own difference stays vague.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence positioning you as the deliberate alternative to the market leader, for a specific kind of buyer they currently serve badly.

sparks.hook: A position lives in the customer's language, not your strategy document.
sparks.insight: Companies routinely write positioning statements full of words no customer has ever said out loud — scalable, holistic, end to end. Those words feel safe internally because they offend nobody and commit to nothing. A real position has to be sayable by a buyer to a colleague in one breath, using words already in their vocabulary. If your position cannot survive being repeated by someone who does not work for you, it is not a position, it is an internal mood.
sparks.why: Positions propagate by repetition through people who are not paid to remember them. Vocabulary that is unfamiliar or abstract does not survive that transmission, however accurate it may be.
sparks.apply: Record two customers describing what you do, then rewrite your positioning line using only words that actually appeared in their answers.

carousel.title: Record real answers
carousel.body: Ask ten customers what you do and why they chose you. Record it. Do not paraphrase, because the paraphrase will drift toward your own internal vocabulary.

carousel.title: Collect repeated words
carousel.body: Mark the words appearing across several answers. Frequency signals that a word already belongs to the category's shared language rather than to you alone.

carousel.title: Delete your jargon
carousel.body: Strike every term no customer used. Words that survive only because a founder likes them are the ones that stop a position from spreading.

carousel.title: Test the sentence
carousel.body: Say the rewritten line to someone outside the company and ask them to repeat it an hour later. If it survives that, it can travel on its own.

sparks.hook: Repetition is not a lack of imagination. It is the whole mechanism.
sparks.insight: Marketers get bored of their own message roughly a hundred times faster than the market absorbs it. The internal impulse is to refresh, rebrand and try a new angle each year, which restarts the memory clock every time. Holding a single consistent claim for years is unexciting work and it is what actually builds a position, because a position is nothing more than a claim repeated long enough and consistently enough to become a fact in somebody's head.
sparks.why: Familiarity builds through repeated exposure and decays without it. Since staff exposure to a message is vastly higher than any customer's, internal boredom is a terrible signal for when to change it.
sparks.apply: Find out how long your current positioning line has been unchanged. If it is under two years, resist changing it and increase how often it appears instead.

sparks.hook: Your name is doing more work than your advertising.
sparks.insight: A name that describes the category, or that people can spell and say, gives you a head start no budget can buy back. Names that are vague, unpronounceable or shared with three other firms create a permanent friction tax on every recommendation, search and conversation about you. This matters more now than it did in 1981, not less, because a customer who cannot spell your name cannot find you, and word of mouth passes through a search box far more often than it used to.
sparks.why: Names affect recall, search and referral, and the cost of a bad one compounds silently. The claim is more defensible today than when it was written, since spoken recommendations now usually end in typing.
sparks.apply: Say your product name to someone unfamiliar and ask them to type it. Every hesitation is friction you are paying for on every single referral.

sparks.hook: The mind rejects anything that clashes with what it already holds.
sparks.insight: If a buyer already believes your category is expensive, or that your kind of company is slow, a message contradicting that belief does not get evaluated on its merits — it gets discarded as implausible. So the workable move is rarely a head-on argument. It is to find the existing belief that supports you and connect to that instead, or to change the category the buyer is filing you under so their prior stops applying. Arguing with a settled belief is the most expensive form of marketing.
sparks.why: People weigh new information against existing beliefs and discount what conflicts. This is well established, though the popular version overstates how fixed beliefs are; they do shift, just slowly and rarely because of an advertisement.
sparks.apply: Write down the one thing your buyer already believes that makes your pitch hard to accept, then build your message on a different belief they already hold.

sparks.hook: Most positioning failures are refusals to give something up.
sparks.insight: Every real position sacrifices customers, use cases or revenue. Leadership meetings that agree on a position in the morning and reject each of its consequences in the afternoon are common, and they end with a message so broad it can be neither wrong nor memorable. The test of whether you have actually positioned anything is simple: name the business you will now decline. If nothing is being declined, you have written a description rather than made a choice.
sparks.why: A claim that excludes nothing distinguishes nothing. Sacrifice is what makes a position credible to buyers and defensible internally when the next tempting opportunity comes along.
sparks.apply: Name the specific customer type or revenue line you will turn away in order to hold your position, and tell your sales team about it this week.

actions: Interview ten customers, record how they describe your category and your product, and rewrite your positioning line using only the words they used.
Write five narrower definitions of your market and pick the one where you could honestly claim to be the leading choice for a real group of buyers.
Name the customer segment or revenue line you will decline in order to hold your position, and communicate that decision to your sales team in writing.
Freeze your positioning line for two years and increase how often it appears, instead of refreshing it whenever the marketing team gets bored of it.
not_for_you_if: You need current examples and evidence — the case studies are early-eighties American brands, many of them long gone, and the tone is assertive rather than researched.

verification.notes: Published 1981, developed from articles the authors wrote in the early 1970s. Examples are dated, and the blanket opposition to line extension is not supported by later evidence. All prose here is original.

title: Contagious
subtitle: Why Things Catch On
author: Jonah Berger
why_it_matters: It replaced the vague idea of virality with six testable properties of things people pass on, backed by a marketing academic's own experiments. It remains the most usable account of why one message travels and a near-identical one dies.

crux.headline: Things spread because of design, not luck alone
crux.body: Sharing is a social act. People pass on what makes them look good, what is triggered by something in their day, what carries feeling, what is publicly visible, what is practically useful, and what arrives inside a story. Most content misses on all six and is then described as unlucky. Engineer even two of them deliberately and you shift the odds, though luck still does a great deal of the work.

sparks.hook: People do not share things. They share things that make them look good.
sparks.insight: Every time someone passes on an article, a product or a recommendation, they are making a small statement about themselves: I know this, I found this first, I have taste. That means the practical question is not whether your thing is interesting to you, but whether repeating it does something for the person repeating it. Anything that makes the sharer look informed, generous or amusing has a strong tailwind. Anything that makes them look like an advertisement has none.
sparks.why: This is the most robust part of the framework: self-presentation drives sharing across studies of conversation and online behaviour. It also explains why referral schemes paying cash often underperform ones that confer status.
sparks.apply: Take your last piece of marketing and ask what a person gains socially by passing it on. If the honest answer is nothing, rewrite it until there is something.

sparks.hook: Six properties separate the message that travels from the one that dies.
sparks.insight: There is no magic to contagion, but there is a checklist. Does sharing it make someone look good? Is there something in ordinary life that will remind people of it? Does it produce real feeling, especially high-energy feeling? Can it be seen being used? Is it useful enough to pass on as a favour? Is it wrapped in a story worth retelling? Most campaigns hit none of these and rely on spend instead. Deliberately building in two or three changes the odds considerably.
sparks.why: The six factors synthesise existing social psychology with the author's own studies of what people email and discuss. They are largely correlational, so treat them as design levers rather than guaranteed causes.
sparks.apply: Score your next campaign out of six against these properties before launch, and refuse to ship anything that scores below two of them.

carousel.title: Give them currency
carousel.body: Build in something that makes the sharer look like an insider: a surprising fact, early access, a detail most people do not know. Nobody passes on what makes them look ordinary.

carousel.title: Attach a trigger
carousel.body: Link the idea to something common in daily life — a time, a food, a routine — so the environment reminds people of you when you are nowhere near them.

carousel.title: Provoke a feeling
carousel.body: Aim for high-arousal emotions like awe, anger or amusement. Sadness is felt just as strongly and shared far less, because it does not create the urge to act.

carousel.title: Make it visible
carousel.body: Design the product or behaviour so it can be seen being used. What is observable gets imitated; what happens privately has to be described, and description is effort.

carousel.title: Make it useful
carousel.body: Practical value travels as a favour between people. A concrete saving or a genuinely helpful tip gets forwarded by people who would never forward an advertisement.

sparks.hook: Triggers beat catchiness. What people see decides what they mention.
sparks.insight: A message that people love but nothing reminds them of will fade within days. A duller message tied to something they encounter constantly — a moment in the morning, a common object, a phrase they hear at work — keeps resurfacing without any further spend. This is why the most memorable campaign is not always the most effective one. Frequency of the reminder in ordinary life often matters more than how clever the thing was when they first met it.
sparks.why: Cues in the environment reliably prompt related thoughts, an effect well documented in memory research. The practical version is that linking to a frequent cue buys you free repetition indefinitely.
sparks.apply: Pick one thing your customer sees or does daily and tie your message to it explicitly, so the object does the reminding on your behalf.

sparks.hook: Anger and awe travel. Sadness, felt just as strongly, does not.
sparks.insight: What predicts sharing is not how strong an emotion is but how activating it is. States that make the body want to do something — outrage, wonder, excitement, anxiety, amusement — push people toward action, and one available action is passing it on. Calm states do the opposite, even when they are deep. This explains why so much of what circulates online is enraging rather than important, and why touching, sad stories often get read widely but forwarded rarely.
sparks.why: Berger's analysis of what readers emailed from a major newspaper's website found high-arousal content shared more, and later work has broadly supported the arousal account. It also explains a fair share of platform toxicity.
sparks.apply: Before publishing, name the exact emotion you expect and whether it makes a reader want to move. If it is calm, add stakes or contrast.

sparks.hook: Behaviour that cannot be seen cannot be copied.
sparks.insight: People take a lot of their cues from what others visibly do, which means anything private is at a permanent disadvantage. Making usage observable — a mark on the product, a shareable artefact, a visible ritual, a public default — converts each customer into a small, silent advertisement that costs nothing to run. The design question is simple and almost never asked: what does a stranger see when someone uses this, and does it say anything at all?
sparks.why: Observational learning is one of the better-supported findings in social psychology. Visibility also solves a hard marketing problem, because it shows real behaviour rather than a claim about behaviour.
sparks.apply: Find one moment where your product is used invisibly and add something a bystander could notice — packaging, a sound, a mark, a shareable result.

sparks.hook: Useful things get forwarded by people who never forward advertising.
sparks.insight: Practical value spreads through a different channel than entertainment: it moves as a favour. Someone sends a colleague a genuinely helpful guide because it makes them a helpful person, and there is no social cost even if the guide is commercial. The condition is that the usefulness must be real and specific — a concrete number, a step that saves an afternoon, a comparison that settles a decision. Vague helpfulness is indistinguishable from marketing and gets treated as such.
sparks.why: Passing on useful information is a low-cost way to invest in a relationship, which is why practical content circulates in professional networks even when it is obviously branded.
sparks.apply: Write one piece of content so specifically useful that a customer could send it to a colleague with no explanation attached at all.

sparks.hook: Wrap the message in a story, or people keep the story and drop you.
sparks.insight: Stories are how information travels between people, so a fact that lives inside a good story gets carried further than one that does not. But there is a catch most campaigns ignore: the story must not work without the product. If the amusing part can be retold with your brand removed, it will be, and you will have paid for entertainment that carries no message at all. The brand has to be load-bearing in the plot, not decoration around the edge of it.
sparks.why: Retelling strips out anything not needed for the story to make sense. That is the mechanism behind memorable adverts nobody can attribute, a well-documented and very expensive failure mode.
sparks.apply: Tell your story to someone and have them retell it a day later. If your product falls out of their version, the story is built wrong.

carousel.title: Find the real detail
carousel.body: Start from something true and specific about how the product came to be, or what it did for someone. Invented drama is easy to spot and expensive when caught.

carousel.title: Make the brand structural
carousel.body: Build the plot so the product causes the interesting turn. If the anecdote still works without you, the retelling will quietly delete you from it.

carousel.title: Cut to retellable length
carousel.body: A story that survives passing between people is short enough to tell in under a minute and contains one surprise, not four competing ones.

carousel.title: Test the retelling
carousel.body: Have someone repeat it a day later without prompting. Whatever they drop is the part you should not have paid to produce.

sparks.hook: Telling people that most others do the wrong thing makes it worse.
sparks.insight: Campaigns often warn that a large share of people behave badly — littering, wasting energy, missing appointments — in the hope of shaming them. It backfires, because the message actually received is that this behaviour is normal, and people follow what appears normal. The effective version says the opposite: name the majority who already do the right thing, and make that majority visible. Social proof works in whichever direction you point it, including the one you did not intend.
sparks.why: Cialdini and colleagues showed this reversal in field studies of littering and hotel towel reuse, and the effect has been repeated in energy-use interventions. It is one of the more reliable findings in this area.
sparks.apply: Check your messaging for any statistic about how many people do the wrong thing, and replace it with the number who already do the right one.

sparks.hook: Most viral hits were not planned, and the planned ones are the exception.
sparks.insight: The honest version of this field is that variance dominates. Content features shift the odds, sometimes substantially, but the distribution of outcomes is extremely skewed and much of what determines a hit is timing, seeding and luck you cannot buy. The productive use of a framework like this is not to manufacture a phenomenon. It is to stop shipping things that had no chance — the messages with no trigger, no feeling, no social payoff and no story.
sparks.why: Studies of information cascades find that repeated runs of the same content produce wildly different outcomes, which limits predictability. Design raises the floor far more reliably than it raises the ceiling.
sparks.apply: Judge your campaigns on the share of content that gets any organic passing on, not on whether one thing went unusually large.

sparks.hook: Word of mouth is mostly offline, and most of it is not about brands.
sparks.insight: The mental image of sharing is a screen, but the large majority of recommendations still happen in person — a comment at work, an answer to a question, a remark in a car. Offline conversation is slower, less measurable and considerably more persuasive, because it comes with a face attached. Building for spread therefore means giving people something easy to say out loud, not only something easy to click, and accepting that the most valuable channel is the one you cannot instrument.
sparks.why: Survey work consistently finds most brand conversation happens face to face rather than online. Measurable channels attract the budget precisely because they are measurable, not because they carry more influence.
sparks.apply: Write the one sentence you want a customer to say out loud about you, and check it is short enough to survive being spoken in a busy room.

actions: Score your next three pieces of marketing against the six sharing properties and refuse to ship anything that scores below two of them.
Identify one thing your customers encounter every day and deliberately attach your message to it so that the environment does the reminding.
Replace every statistic in your communications about how many people do the wrong thing with one about the majority already doing the right thing.
Tell your brand story to a colleague, ask them to retell it a day later, and rewrite it if your product disappears from their version.
not_for_you_if: You want a repeatable formula for guaranteed virality, or you distrust popular-psychology framings built on correlational studies and selected case examples.

verification.notes: Published 2013 by Simon & Schuster. The six-factor framework synthesises existing social psychology with Berger's own studies; findings are largely correlational and virality remains heavily luck-driven. All prose here is original.

title: Made to Stick
subtitle: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die
author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
why_it_matters: It took the question of why some ideas stick and turned it into six concrete properties a writer or manager can check before speaking. It changed how a generation of executives, teachers and journalists structure a message.

crux.headline: Ideas stick when they are simple, concrete and human
crux.body: A memorable idea is rarely the most complete one. It is stripped to a single core claim, made unexpected enough to hold attention, described in things people can picture, backed by something credible they can check themselves, connected to a feeling about a person rather than a number, and delivered inside a story. None of that is talent. It is a checklist you can run on any message before you send it.

sparks.hook: The more you know, the worse you get at explaining it.
sparks.insight: Once you understand something deeply, you cannot easily reconstruct what it is like not to. Your explanations skip steps, lean on jargon that feels ordinary to you, and start in the middle. This is why experts consistently overestimate how clear they are being, and why the person who understands a subject best is often the worst person to introduce it. The remedy is not simplification for its own sake — it is deliberately rebuilding the path a newcomer has to walk.
sparks.why: In a well-known Stanford study, people tapping out familiar tunes on a table vastly overestimated how often listeners would identify them. Knowing the tune made silence feel like melody, which is exactly the trap.
sparks.apply: Explain your idea to someone outside your field and ask them to repeat it back. Rewrite every part they could not reproduce accurately.
